scope: generic transferable interaction knowledge only; no target-game observations, solutions, state signatures, action outcomes, or labels

memories.instruction: Game Boy convention: D-pad usually supplies four directions; A/B usually supply primary/secondary actions; Start/Select usually handle start, pause, menu, or selection. Treat this only as a weak mapping prior and verify from state changes.

NES convention: D-pad usually supplies four directions; A/B usually supply action controls; Start/Select usually handle game or menu functions. Treat this only as a weak mapping prior and verify from feedback.

SNES convention: D-pad usually supplies directions; A/B/X/Y are action candidates; L/R are additional action candidates; Start/Select are usually system or menu controls. Verify every mapping in the current game.

Xbox-style convention: left stick or D-pad often controls movement/navigation; right stick often controls camera/aim; A/B/X/Y, bumpers, and triggers are action candidates; Menu/View are usually system controls. Verify from observed effects.

PC convention: WASD or arrows often control movement; mouse movement often points or aims; mouse buttons, Space, Enter, Shift, Ctrl, and number keys are common action candidates; Escape often means pause/back. Verify rather than assume.

For an unknown game, first discover what is controllable and which actions change state. Set a provisional short-term goal from observable progress. If repeated actions in an equivalent state produce no useful change, revise the action or goal. Promote explicit success or progression signals when discovered.

Use interaction-design priors: visible/spatial elements may offer affordances; compare before/after state for feedback; no effect may mean boundary, obstacle, precondition, wrong context, or inactive control; probe unresolved controls systematically; reuse mappings that remain consistent.

Use game-design priors: games usually have learnable rules and an explicit or implicit goal; objects may be targets, resources, obstacles, hazards, switches, or decoration; score, new area, capability, persistent state change, or level transition may signal progress; preserve before-action-after evidence to infer rules.
